name: Laya vs CrossEncoder
intro:
Eight payment intents. Four systems.
Accuracy, calibration, and measured CPU latency.
version: Repository experiment · protocol and interpretation limits in the full report

chapters.title:
Eight intents.
One fixed test set.
chapters.subtitle: A BANKING77 subset, not the full task.
paragraphs: The protocol uses eight related payment intents, 50 allocated training and 20 validation requests per intent, and all 40 official test requests for each selected intent.
The held-out test set contains 320 requests. All reported systems use the same test rows, question wording, and option descriptions.
chapters.note: The benchmark does not establish performance across all 77 intents or on out-of-scope requests.

chapters.title:
An option question.
Eight pair scores.
chapters.subtitle: Read the unit of computation.
paragraphs: Laya scores a single question with eight options. Each CrossEncoder scores eight request–option pairs. Both turn their outputs into a decision over the same intents.
The checkpoints, heads, and training histories differ. Even the large-encoder comparison is a system comparison, not an isolated Decision Head ablation.
chapters.note: Do not attribute the entire accuracy difference to architecture.

chapters.title:
Count the
correct decisions.
chapters.subtitle: From 248 to 290 correct Laya predictions.
paragraphs: Original Laya reached 77.5% accuracy; fine-tuned Laya reached 90.6%. ModernBERT-base CrossEncoder reached 89.7%, and the large CrossEncoder reached 93.4%.
The large CrossEncoder was correct on nine more of the 320 requests than fine-tuned Laya: 299 versus 290.
chapters.note: One test split is not a reliable universal ranking of these systems.

chapters.title:
A percentage is
not the whole comparison.
chapters.subtitle: Probability quality and CPU time also matter.
paragraphs: Fine-tuned Laya took 98.8 ms/request in the recorded CPU run, compared with 208.0 ms for the large CrossEncoder. The base CrossEncoder took 76.3 ms.
Probability metrics tell another part of the story: log loss, Brier score, and ECE should be read beside accuracy, with their calibration protocols in view.
chapters.note: All timings are single local CPU runs with batch size four, not hardware-independent throughput claims.

chapters.title:
Compare systems.
Avoid a causal shortcut.
chapters.subtitle: The training protocols are not identical.
paragraphs: Laya held back 40 of its 400 allocated training items for calibration, leaving 360 gradient-training items. CrossEncoder used all 400 and fitted temperature on validation logits.
Starting checkpoints, heads, and objectives also differ. The report documents frequent intent confusions and the remaining limits of the comparison.
chapters.note: A controlled architecture ablation would need matched initialization, training, and evaluation conditions.
